And each time I wrote a new book, my guiding lights were this: number one, either no book existed with that information in it, or [number two] no book existed where that information was all under one cover. So I started to write. I’m not even sure what the order is. I wrote the improvisation book. I think the next book I wrote was a book called Composition for the . . .
I think the Arranging and Composing for the Small Ensemble [book] was . . .

That’s what I was about to say – was the second book. Then, each time there was a need – you know, Jamey [Aebersold] proceeded along these same lines. Sometimes I could see that Jamey was using the models that I had set, and then he translated them into play-alongs, which was great. Fact is, we even coincided one time, when I wrote the II-V book [Techniques of Improvisation. Volume 2: The II V7 Progression]. It had a green and white cover, and all of a sudden the green and white cover of the [II-V7 play-along] record was the same [colors]. So always my writing – particularly in these kinds of books – was driven by necessity, by the fact that no books existed. Now, on other levels, for instance the pedagogy book, which to my knowledge was the first book on pedagogy – jazz pedagogy – written, was one that was driven by the fact that people were worrying me to death every summer. “Can you send me your syllabuses?” “Can you tell me how you do this?” “What do you do in an arranging class?” “How do you plan a recital?” And I kept thinking, if I’m going to be sending out xeroxes of that information, why don’t I just put it in a book? So each book came at a time when there was no such book available or where that information was not all under one cover. Then I began to diversify so that I began writing about things other than “how to.” There were essays on philosophical concerns about the music. For instance, that had been the first article that I had written for Down

Beat, the article called Jazz: the Academy’s Neglected Stepchild. It was a chance to get on the soapbox and talk about the fact that jazz education and jazz educators had to begin dealing with American music, specifically jazz music. It didn’t win me a lot of friends, but it did break ground and did get people thinking about it. In there I criticized not only the educational system, but I criticized racial attitudes – the fact that I was looking at the various camps that were in existence, and I looked to see people running things, and I didn’t see black faces. It was no attempt to make it exclusively black, but only simply to say that it seemed to be very ridiculous that in a music created out of black culture, that there were so few blacks involved in it in any meaningful way in decision-making processes. So I wrote a lot of philosophical books. I edited a lot of books. I had sporadic columns in Down Beat and a continuing column in The Jazz Player [magazine] later on. And I started to think in terms of the areas. I began to get grants and also appointments to travel and do lectures. And every time I would do a lecture, that would become a point of study for me, to really prepare the lecture. So I was doing lectures. I did a lecture when I traveled on one of the big – what was it? The Rock – it wasn’t Rockefeller. It was – the grant where I did bebop and took it into the various colleges. It doesn’t matter [that I can't remember the name]. At any rate, I did a lot of those, and I found that they were the things that were driving my writing, my literary writing. When somebody said they didn’t know something, I would study it in much the same way as when I get ready to write a concerto. If it’s for an instrument I haven’t written for, I’ll spend an inordinate amount of time studying people who have written those, studying music that’s a saxophone concerto, or whatever, before I write. I do the same thing when I write books. This is the longest I’ve ever gone in my life without writing a book, since I started writing books. I think the last book I wrote was How to – not how to practice . . .
How to Learn Tunes, I think, was the last one.

How to Learn Tunes was the last book, and that’s been what? Three or four years. I have four or five books in my head now. I have a how to teach book which deals with the vagaries of today: how to deal with harassment, how to deal with changing attitudes in students. The book is ready to go, but I haven’t sat down to write the book. There’s a book on how to write music that’s in the Thirdstream vein. That’s in preparation. It’s ready to go. I haven’t had time to sit down and write the book, which would have been probably the best argument for retirement, but unfortunately, for me, everything I do is driven by what I do in the classroom. If I weren’t in the classroom, then probably the books wouldn’t be there in my mind.

So I feel that my books, Jerry Coker’s books, George Russell’s book, [and] Jamey Aebersold’s play-alongs have laid pretty much the foundation for jazz education. A lot of people don’t know this or don’t choose to acknowledge it, but when I go places, I think the people that I really respect are very aware of that foundation and that they’re going to my books. For a long time I would check attributions, and I would see, in book after book, my books being listed as source material. Dissertations – it’s almost impossible to find a dissertation on jazz that doesn’t list at least one of my books and books by Jerry Coker, which is I think the final proof of whether a book is valuable and how it is being used, because those citations tell you how much the book is being used. I’ve got a lot of students who borrow very liberally without attribution, but I’ve got a lot of other students who do give attribution to the books. I never have to worry about Jerry Coker or people who are experienced people plagiarizing. Sometimes people don’t even bother to re-state. I won’t say who, but I can remember, like, 25 years ago, somebody who has since become quite a good educator, borrowing whole sections of my improvisation book. I called Down Beat and said, “I won’t accept this. You’ve got to go to them and get them to admit” – and of course the cat came clean. Maybe he thought I wasn’t going to see the book. I don’t know. So I’ve become a stickler, since I’ve been an educator, for honesty in writing, that when I have an idea, like this whole notion of the use of the word “contrafact,” I go back to [James] Patrick, because that’s a word that he coined to use for this. It came from an earlier word – I mean, used differently in earlier times, but I always credit him with that.
James Patrick.

I try to give credit always when I use material, and I’m always upset when I don’t see that credit. I’m always very suspicious when I see a book that doesn’t have an index, because it tells me that somebody didn’t take the time . . .
Bibliography.

No, I meant index – I want to know when I look in the back that the people have taken the time to say where I can find information that I’m looking for on a given page. I want a bibliography and a discography too, but the index – I really mean index. I want to go alphabetically and see if my name is in the book. I want to see if Jerry Coker’s name is in the book. So I mean index. Okay?

In a book that’s a scholarly book, I want to also see discographical sources, I want to see a bibliography, and I want to see footnotes. I want to see those things. But it starts with me, if it’s a scholarly book, with looking in the index, because that’s the first place I look. If I don’t see my name in the book and it’s a book about something that I know I’ve written a lot about, then I start to look to see, what did he say about it? Then sometimes I can see full paragraphs that were just simply lifted and not even restated. Then I can get mad and get over it and go on to the next book, you dig? So I feel like I’ve had an influence on education simply because I’ve written so many books, and so many of the books were at a time when there were no other books, no competing books. That of course diminishes as you see more and more people writing books. I’m amazed at how often – I can never forget Ted Dunbar going after Gary Campbell. Gary’s one of my students and somebody I respect and love very much, but he came here, and he brought a book that he had just published with Jim Houston. We were downstairs [in my studio] with Dottie – Ted’s girlfriend – and Lida and myself and Luke Gillespie and some others, and we were going to play. He brought the book over, and he showed it to Ted. He said, “Here’s my new book.” And Ted reamed him out. He said, “Man, how can you write a book here? Everything in here is something David just gave you.” Ted would get very protective of me. And when he got done, the next edition of that book had the attributions in it. Sometimes it’s not calculated. People are not being malicious. They just don’t think about it. And you know, I think, too, that the statement that says, “Being original means choosing obscure sources” – sometimes people really think, "Well, nobody’s ever seen this book, so if I say something out of this book, they won’t know where it came from." But I fortunately have something close to total recall once I read a book. That’s why kids can’t get away with – I don’t even bother to ask them to write papers in my big classes anymore, because I can remember where I saw it. Then they’re in deep trouble, so I just don’t ask for them. I think the most valuable asset that a teacher has is a good and accurate recall system, because you’ve got to remember when you need metaphors, when you need analogies, when you need examples, you’ve got to be able to reach back in your mind and find out what best exemplifies this thing. Every time I run into a situation I haven’t encountered before, it goes into the file cabinet so I can call it forth when I need it. I think if you don’t have that, you run the risk of not being able to teach. I love those situations where I’m stumped – when I’m working with a student and they’re doing everything I tell them and they’re not making any progress – because then I’ve got to go back to the drawing board and try to figure another way to do it. Once in a while I get a student who will challenge me beyond belief. Ralph Bowen was one of those. I couldn’t figure why – I would have to stay up nights before Ralph [would get

here]. He was [studying] on the Canadian Arts Council grant. The week before he would come, I’d have to start trying to figure what the hell I was going to do with him when he got here. Then – because, when he asked me to take him as a student, I said no, because I didn’t know him. [Then] I said, “Okay, I’ll let you come down once and I’ll try it.” Then I can remember Pat LaBarbera saying to me at Louisville – he said, “How do you like that student I sent you, Ralph Bowen?” I said, “You did this to me.” And he said, “Yeah, I got tired of trying to dream up what to do with him.” And now I got another student, a little violinist named Billy Contreras, who is the same way. I have to stay up trying to think. I welcome those challenges, because then you’ve got to find a way. Delfayo [Marsalis] presented some of those challenges. I would have to think of, what am I going to do with him? What would benefit him the most? He’s already playing with Elvin [Jones]. Now what? What do I do? We would – I’d stay up at nights. We would try things. I would have – I would do things to force his mind. I would say, “I tell you what. Here’s a tune that’s 16 bars long, and here’s a blues that’s 12 measures long. I want you to play the blues changes across this whole tune and make it fit.” The tune would come together every third chorus, I mean where [bar] one was again, because 12, 12, 12 is like 16, 16. I would work these kinds of things or whatever. But you’re forever trying to find different ways, which is why I had to keep teaching, because my own playing is dependent on my teaching, man, because I work on everything that I assign. And sometimes I forget. “Damn. You know, I have forgotten to do this. I haven’t done this in a long time.” Then I sit down there [in my studio] with that cello, boy, and I try to get myself ready, so that the next time I encounter the tune . . . And I have some other things. For instance, my students – and when you hear people talk about it, it means they’ve gone to my how-to-practice book [A Creative Approach to Practicing Jazz]. I always tell everybody, the tune you work on the next day is the tune that you didn’t know the night before. You ain't gonna never get me on a tune twice. You might find a tune I don’t know, but when you call that tune the next time, I know that tune in all keys. You’ll get me on another tune, probably, but I’m going to learn that tune, so that every time you’re building a cumulative experience. So basically I try to think along those lines when I’m dealing with students and in my own thinking and my practicing. They then ultimately become books. Everybody kept asking me, "how do you practice this?" "How do you practice this?" "How do you practice this?" Sometimes, even after they get the book – [James] Moody called me two weeks ago and said, “David, I really need some help.” He said, “I got your book on how to practice,” he said, “but I can’t seem to get myself organized about how to get the most out of my practice.” Then we sit down, and we go through the book. And I talk about, “Well, here’s a page. Here’s something have you ever tried?” For instance, when

I’m playing, some days I don’t feel like playing scales and all that. So what I’ll do is take one tune, or take one key. And I say I’m going to play every tune that I practice today in that key. Or I’m going to play every tune that I play that day starting on A-flat. So it’s throwing me in all kinds of keys, because if I start on A-flat and I’m playing Misty, that throws me into the key of D-flat [Baker sings “Ab-F-C” and continues the opening phrase of Misty], or whatever. But if I take How High the Moon and I start on A-flat, I’m in D-flat. If I start [I’m] Getting Sentimental Over You, I’m in the key of A major, because it’s G# [Baker sings "G#-A-C#-E-G#"]. Or if I’m playing Misty – or The Shadow of Your Smile, and I have to make that adjustment. Or sometimes I’ll play all the tunes that have “spring” in the title or “fall” in the title. And now you’ve got a double whammy, because not only are you trying to think of where the tune starts, but then you’re trying to think of tunes. How many tunes can you name? Can you name 20 tunes? I have a thing with the students that I take. They have to learn the 34 bebop tunes first, because that’s the foundation. [Baker has a list of 34 tunes that exemplify the essential bebop vocabulary.] I say, “If anything happened to me tomorrow, or you had to leave and go somewhere else, if you knew those 34 bebop tunes, you’d be ready to play.” It's that stack I gave you, [James]. James Zimmerman: Yes.

If I get somebody who can do that, man, I can teach him the rest pretty easily, because I’ve given him all the vocabulary. And I tell them it’s always cumulative. For instance, one of the reasons why it’s possible in the English language to count to a million – you don’t need to know but 1 to 9 and zero. That’s all you need to know. If you had to learn a different digit, it would go 1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8-9-pick-flank-snick-snort­ crook-cricket-purpa-fribble-zinka-booma. Pretty soon you wouldn’t remember anything. It's why they tell you, like when they give you telephone numbers and they give you social security numbers, that our capacity usually is limited to 3 plus 3 plus 4. If you look at your social security number, it’s broken up a different way, and you look at your thing – it’s getting more than that now because of what’s happening with the internet and that stuff, but generally speaking, that’s as much as you can remember unless it’s in sequence. They’ve done the studies, the tests, to tell you that. As a teacher, I’ve got to know that when I make an assignment, or [am] telling somebody to remember something, or give them a way to remember tunes. If I’m telling somebody – they’re learning a tune, and they’re learning the changes – if I tell them that here are 25 tunes that the "A" section is the same changes as Take the “A” Train, man, I’ve done them a service. They ain’t got to learn that shit over and over. And I’m too lazy to learn anything that I can only use in one circumstance. I don’t even want to hear it. Don’t give me a word that I can’t use every – that’s why I don’t want to know about supercalifragilisticexpialodocious. I can’t use it. Where am I going to use it? In the

middle of a conversation? I’m trying to talk some shit to somebody, and I stick that in there? They think I’m nuts. So when I learn words and when I teach, I have people learn things that they can use. If you can use them immediately and continue to use them – how many times when you get ready to take a solo have you found yourself – you hear somebody play something and you say, “I used to do that when I played”? So what I try to do is keep it in a rotation, so if I hear – give me a glance at it, it brings back all the things that go with it. I wanted to make up some games that would be, like, syndicated games, where you had to have enough of a vocabulary that if a cat sang a lick from a tune, you had to tell him what was the lick that came from the phrase just before that, or if he sang a phrase, you had to sing the phrase that went before it in the tune. So you hear [Baker sings bars 3-4 of Joy Spring]. What’s the next phrase? [Baker sings bars 3-4 again.] Or the phrase that comes before it? [Baker sings bars 1-4 of Joy Spring]. I want them to sing that. Or they go [Baker sings bars 5-6]. Or I sing the first 8 [bars]. We got hung up, man, doing this with David Lahm, I couldn’t [remember] for the life of me – none of us [could] – and I said, "the last phrase of the bridge is 'and what’s more she’s got arms.' " We went around a whole evening trying to remember what tune it was. Do you know what it is? [Baker sings] “And what’s more she’s got arms.”
Love Is Just Around the Corner.

Love Is Just Around the Corner. [Baker sings] “Venus de Milo was noted for her charms. But strictly between us, you’re cuter than Venus, and what’s more you’ve got arms.” I would play this game with Patty Coker. James Zimmerman: It's called what?
Love Is Just Around the Corner.

Love Is Just Around the Corner. I would play the game with Patty Coker, and we would go at it. She would sing a phrase, and I’d have to sing the next line. Or Jerry [Coker] would sing a phrase. [Baker sings a phrase]. The next phrase is [the Bakers sing it together]. Miles [Davis]. Or you hear [Baker sings the beginning of Miles's solo from So What]. That’s So What. And, again, you start to sharpen your perception, but it’s always a constant battle. Like I said, [it's] like lifting weights. If you lift weights and you’re lifting 150 pounds every day, all you do is stay basically on the same plateau. But if you start every week adding two more repetitions or adding two more pounds – somebody told the story, man, of a cat

who ultimately was able to lift a bull by standing on the thing every day with a pulley under that calf when it was a calf. Every day he lifted the calf, every day. When it got to be a bull, he could still lift it, because he had never felt the change. You dig? Now you can get a hernia . . . [laughter] But again, what I’m saying is I write books that are challenging books, and I never write a book that covers something that I feel like is already covered very, very well. I don’t bother with that. That’s why people get headaches trying to deal with that book like the advanced concepts. Moody told me the other day, he said, “You know, I live in that book,” [Techniques of Improvisation. Volume 4: Cycles] and then Nathan [Davis] said, “Me, too.” And I can hear it in their playing.
It’s the contemporary techniques book.
It’s part of the [Techniques of Improvisation] series.

One other thing that I wanted to cover with you was the evolution of what is now the International Association of Jazz Educators [International Association for Jazz Education]. You were a part of that almost from the beginning. Now [as president-elect] you’re going to be incorporating your vision into what’s going to be happening in the future with that organization. Could you speak a little bit about that?

First of all, it was a long time aborning. We were a part of MENC, which is the Music Educators National Conference. I can remember in Chicago, when we first began to talk about this with Leon Breeden, with Matt Betton, with Stan Kenton. That picture you saw in my book, that was [a photograph] from that conference. We began talking about the formation of such an organization. I didn’t follow through about it, because it was just an idea. Matt Betton and the rest of them did. They started the organization [NAJE: National Association of Jazz Educators], and it started as a mom and pop organization. You thought little, and you did little. We were still an arm of the MENC. Then they broke away from the MENC. [They] still remained basically a mom and pop organization for years, because they thought small. I can remember one of the most dramatic breakthroughs was when they called in the National Jazz Service Organization – Eunice Lockhart-Moss, myself, James Jordan – and asked us to give them some thoughts about how to make this a national organization.
When was that?

It was when the NJSO was still functional. It’s been – so it’s got to have been more than – probably 15 years ago, maybe. I don’t remember for sure. But I remember that’s when they [NAJE] hired an executive director, in Bill McFarlin. That’s when it
ceased to become two people running it. Then I can remember we – it was when we were in Los Angeles. So it’s one of the times when we were in L.A.
When the convention was in L.A. – the NAJE convention, IAJE by then, I think.
No, it was not.
It was still NAJE?

It was NAJE. It did not become IAJE for quite a while. So basically it went through all the growing pains, and it is only within the last 10 years that they began to draw in international kind of things and also having the kind of sponsorship where people felt there were enough people and it was prestigious enough that they could send their record company to pay – because they don’t pay anybody to play or be there. So all of a sudden you have to be able to attract – know that there is a track record before people are willing to send somebody from Columbia Records, and schools are starting to have booths. Now, you know, we’re at, what? There are people from, what? How many people were at this last one? They said 8,000 people from 160 countries? I thought, boy, this is really great. So it’s been a long time moving from the mom and pop organization to the National Jazz Service Organization [Baker means the International Association for Jazz Education]. I wish I could think of all the people that are in the picture [photograph]. It was Kenton. It was Matt Betton. It was the guy who is from upstate New York – nice looking guy with a round face. He’s still an active member. He’s a past president of the organization [Lee Bash]. Then they came up with by-laws and guidelines and things that allow them to have president-elect, president, past president, and all the other trappings that go with big time organizations. So basically, all I can say is that it was one of the most valuable things that could have happened to the field, because now that’s almost a must. I went though several years when I wasn’t involved or didn’t get involved, just like [Jerry] Coker never got involved, because I was upset, because it was largely neophonic bands that were patterned after Stan Kenton. There was not much attention being paid to small groups nor to anybody but the white players who’d come out of those kinds of bands. They were mostly teachers without any experiential knowledge. Coker and I were among the first, along with the guy who used to play with Horace Silver, a trumpet player from Michigan, and he never followed through – Smith – Louis Smith – among the first people who were practitioners. Then later on Bunky Green and cats like that who became bigwigs in the organization. I said only kind of jokingly at the keynote [speech I gave at the January 2000 conference] last time that it would become the intergalactic
[Intergalactic Association for Jazz Education] – I don’t know at what point we’ll start getting aliens in there.
They are already there.
Some of them, I think, are hiding in there already.
You served as a vice president in that organization as well.

I was vice president in the organization for two years and chose not to let them put me forward for a presidency at the time, simply because there was turmoil. We had offered the job to David Robinson, Scott’s brother, and then had to rescind the offer, because it hadn’t gone through the proper channels. We were having great financial troubles at the time. I didn’t feel like, without compromising my creative energies, I could take the job at that time, and I said, “No.” When I was approached before Christmas or whenever it was this time, I said, “Let me think about it.” They gave me some guidelines, and I gave them guidelines about what I could and couldn’t do, or would and wouldn’t do. And I think now is a time that – as the oldest person to have been a president in the organization, I bring a lot of experiential knowledge and perhaps vision that they may not have in the younger cats that they’ve had. I think maybe I’m the – I’m parallel – I'm probably the same age as some other people, but I mean, to take the office I’m probably the oldest person, 'cause I will be 70 when I take the office and 72 when I exit the office.
You were notified [the] day before yesterday that you will be the . . .
I told them [Ken and James] that I’m already the new president. I will be the president-elect.
To wrap up, I know you’ve got to be very proud that you’ve got some upcoming generations of musicians in our family.

My daughter chose to go into music, but she chose to go into music at the last minute. When she was getting ready to graduate from high school, she made the decision the last year, because she said she thought I wouldn’t be happy with her if she didn’t do all the same things that I did. I convinced her that was not the case at all. So she took up violin. But when she graduated from college – she was the first string player to graduate from the jazz program [at Indiana University] – when she graduated from college, [and] she even was my teaching assistant while she was a senior, she went to work for J. C. Penney as a buyer – first of all, a sales person, and then as a buyer – and rose very quickly to big money, because she’s got a real knack for it. She was smart

and was doing very, very well in that thing. There was no music at all. She wasn’t doing any music at all. She was simply doing this. And I thought it [was] kind of ironic, because when they had the bi[centennial] – the centennial, or whatever the sesqui[centennial] – whatever it was . . .
Bicentennial of the U.S. in 1976.

I was one of the people that they [the J. C. Penney Company] asked to write music for that. I was the jazz person. I wrote a big piece which was for – Benny Goodman played it. They had all music represented, and they gave all these [away] – gave these [scores and parts for the commissioned compositions] away to all the schools. And then I thought, boy, now here she is, working for J. C. Penney . . .
Because [the J. C.] Penney [Company] was one of the main underwriters of that whole commissioning [program].
No, it wasn’t the main underwriter. It was the only underwriter.
It was the only underwriter?

Yeah. It was J. C. Penney's project. April then came – was working as a buyer and moved to Chicago – to New Palatine [Palatine, Illinois]. Then she got pregnant. She thought she would still put the baby in a . . .
Daycare.

. . . in daycare. I remember getting a call one evening. She said, “Daddy, I want to come home.” I tried to hide my joy, not very well probably. She decided – I said, “If you want to move back, we’ll come up and get you.” So she moved back. For a while it was – I’m not sure – she still was working. She started working down here. Then she decided she was going to take some students, because she had come up with some methods of her own. First thing I knew, she had about 25 vocal students. Then they offered her a job teaching strings in the school system. So now what she does is, she’s got a full studio of vocalists – mostly my college students, vocal students, are her students – and then very young violinists, up to probably [age] 14 or 15. So that’s been very satisfying, because she’s a very serious teacher. She uses my books probably more efficiently than I do, simply because I refer to them, but I wrote them, so I don’t feel like I have to really deal with them in the same way she does. But when somebody comes to her – for instance, Amy Fanning, who’s one of my best students. She is going to be working on a doctorate. She’s got her master’s in jazz studies. But she’s a singer. So she studied with April – her and Dimitri, one of my students from Greece.

She [April] has a six- or seven-point plan. She has them learn, say, Hot House. When they learn Hot House, then they have to learn to sing the roots of the tune without – this is all without piano. Then they have to be able to sing patterns – simple patterns – on the tune. So the tune is [Baker sings] “What is this thing called love?" The changes go [Baker sings] “G minor, C seventh, F minor, B-flat seventh, D minor, G seventh, C" and they’ve got to be able to sing [the roots and note names for each of these chords] [Baker sings] "G, C, F, B-flat, D, G, C." Then next they go [Baker sings a simple pattern of roots and seconds on each of these chords]. Then they go [Baker sings through patterns made up of chord outlines to the seventh, connecting with descending phrases derived from the bebop scale]. She has them go [through] a six-point step before she lets them sing with the piano. Then they sing with the piano, but now they’re singing changes. They know the tune. They can sing on the changes. And she makes them learn them in all keys, because your voice feels different in different keys. And if it’s – she teaches the traditional ballads and stuff, too – style – but it’s been a joy for me, because I learn from her. I learn – 'cause I tend to let people slide. If they’re making the effort, I say, shit, I want to go on to the next thing. [Jerry] Coker was somebody who was a fiend for having everything be perfect before they could move [on]. I tend to be lax about that. I let people move on to the next thing, figuring I can clean it up at some other point. The same thing with her violin players. She uses my – the book that’s called – the one you have – the one that she gave you. The one that's for the violin. It’s called Explorations. Something and explorations. [Jazz Treble Clef Expressions and Explorations] She uses that now to practice, and I see results. Now my granddaughter [Kirsten] – and that’s been really a joy – we bought her a violin about like that [Baker gestures to show the size of the tiny violin] when she was three, because she wanted one for her birthday, and she’s now making it up through the ranks on the violin. She went through a thing this last – she fell in love [with the piano]. We gave her a piano for Christmas, an electric piano. She wants to play Für Elise all day long on that one.
And Heart and Soul.

And boogie woogie and Heart and Soul. So she told her mother, “I hate the violin. I’m not going to play violin. I want to play piano.” Her mother said, “No. If you get the violin together and keep that together, then I’ll give you piano lessons.” [Kirsten said,] “I hate you. I don’t want to do that.” So I bribed her. I said, “Look. You’re going to be switching to the next size violin pretty soon. Every time you have a good lesson, I’m going to give you 'X' amount of dollars." Now she’s really hooked again on the violin, because she’s going up to the next size violin.

But it’s really nice to see the lineage keep going, because – and fortunately, they're – my nephews. I started up all them on [instruments], and they were really bright. Kim could have learned flute in two weeks, if he'd really wanted to. He’s the one who lives in Australia now. David played the trombone. Finally I just let that alone, because it was too much work. But with April, she came voluntarily to it. And Kirsten, she just said, “I want to play.” When she was three years old, on December 11th, her birthday, she got her first violin, and still now plays in little recitals and stuff. So that’s been kind of a reward for me. April sings very well. She doesn’t do that, primarily 'cause she’s a violinist. But she really can sing. I heard her do – what was it? It wasn’t [My] Funny Valentine that she did down there, was it?
Yeah, it was.

And she kicked ass. And, of course, she has her singers imitate. She says, “When you can imitate enough people, then you can find your own self in there somewhere.” So she has them sing until they sound just like Ella [Fitzgerald], or they sound just like Billie Holiday], or they sound just like Tony Bennett. That may be one month. Then the next month they have to sound like somebody else. By the time they’ve done that through six or seven singers, all of a sudden they find out that they’ve got their own shit. And you can tell that they borrowed stuff. So basically, at a time when I’m raising other people’s children daily, it is really nice to see my own child and grandchild doing what they do, 'cause if – I say it caustically to the students when they don’t do what they’re supposed to do, I say, “Look. I ain’t got no time to raise nobody else’s children. Now you either do the stuff or you don’t do it.” And then I make them do it anyway, so . . . [laughter]
How would you like to be remembered? What do you see as your . . .
I don’t like that question. If you ask me what I see as my legacy, that’s one thing.
Well, what do you think have been your major contributions to the field?
Everything we talked about. Education – certainly I think I’m one of the pioneers there. I think probably, if my music continues to get played – the classical

music – I think they will stop the nonsense of believing that people such as Hale [Smith], and I, and Olly [Wilson], and the cats, that we have no place in classical music. I think that’s important, that we persevere and let people know that environment and training are as important as the DNA. That would be something. And I’d like to think that maybe what my grandmother used to say when we were with people, that if you can’t get along with me, you can’t get along with anybody. That would be enough, if I had just that, that people know. Like at my office, there’s 20 people outside the door all the time – people I don’t want to be bothered with, but people that I’ll be bothered with, because they need to have somebody to talk to. It means I don’t have time for myself sometimes, but I think you have to be willing to – I was given a gift, and I know that. And I take very seriously the responsibility of utilizing that gift to its fullest. Sometimes I have to listen to you go through your thing about, “I just can’t keep up. I can’t do this. I can’t listen to music all day long.” [Baker turns to Ken and James] She [Lida] told me, when she wanted a bigger house, “We’re going to have to soundproof that room down there, because I can’t handle it, you getting up at 5 in the morning and playing.” I knew what the ploy was, so we were cool. We didn’t get the bigger house, but we did the house over here, so that was cool.
That’s all I wanted, just some peace and quiet.
Well, you didn’t get the peace and quiet.
No.

And I’m sorry about that, but I did get that funny little cello you all [Ken and James] put together, that don’t make no noise. [laughter] No, I’d rather be remembered as a nice human being than all the other stuff. The other stuff will come if anybody’s interested in it. But just somebody that people liked and somebody who liked people. And I really do like people. I can’t imagine being mad at anybody for any length of time. I’m already over the [Indiana] Pacers [basketball team]. I can get along with them now. I like Reggie [Miller] again. Mark Jackson’s okay. Fact is, I’ve got to tell you this – and it can be on here [on the tape] if you want it – I got a little upset in reading the big article on Larry Bird today, because Larry Bird said something that really bothered me. It’s out of context, when you start talking about, forgetting that it’s a game. Larry said today, he cannot stand the nonsense of people being friends with their adversaries when they play the game. He says he doesn’t like them to shake their hand after the game, and he doesn’t want them hugging and stuff. He said Magic [Johnson] and Isaiah [Thomas] started all this nonsense. He said he wants them to hate the people that they’re playing. He said he did it when he played. He said that business of them hugging each other at the end of the – after the series is over

– he said – and the guy who wrote the article said Jack Nicholson didn’t give him any choice. He reached out there and grabbed him. But I for one cannot imagine that you ever forget that that’s a game, or that you ever forget that music is not everybody’s entire life. When somebody tells me, they don’t want out there – with the exception of Kirsten – then I think that they should do something else, and I think they should not lose the respect of other people because they’re – I don’t think you should force people to do things. I think you can entice them, bribe them, do whatever you are if it looks like it might be in their best interest. But I don’t ever forget that the most important things are family, health, and those things that we have no control over, except in a certain measure. We can eat right. We can do that right. But I ain’t got time to worry about shit that I can’t fix. I get excited about the game and raise hell, but when the game’s over, if they had lost . . .
If the Lakers had lost.

Yeah. I would have found a dog or something and kicked the shit out of him for a minute [laughter]. I’m kidding. Folks, that was a joke [laughter]. I think we’ve got some days of good stuff. You did nice questions.
(transcribed and edited by Barry Kernfeld)
[additional editing by Lida Baker, March 2007]

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Opening of the Smithsonian interview, tape one
segments.summary: Funding credit, interviewee and interviewer details, and Lida Baker's spoken introduction at the Bloomington home on June 19, 2000.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Born on the east side of Indianapolis
segments.summary: Baker was born December 21, 1931 at 24th and Arsenal, near Douglas Park, among neighbors who became jazz musicians such as the Montgomerys, Russell Webster and Gene Fowlkes.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Losing his mother at age four
segments.summary: His mother died of tuberculosis when he was four; he recalls her meticulousness, her apology after the coal chute, and her death reciting the 23rd Psalm.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Father's carpentry and post office work, Depression hardship, stepmother and Aunt Evelyn
segments.summary: His father, trained in carpentry at Hampton, was shut out by a closed shop and took post office work; Depression meals, a stepmother after 1938, weekends with Aunt Evelyn and a wholly black neighborhood, with Armstrong and gospel and country radio heard at home.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Radio listening: Randy's Record Shop, rhythm-and-blues and Nat King Cole
segments.summary: Radio supplied the music: Randy's Record Shop, Louis Jordan, Basie, Nat King Cole, plus the black newspaper and the closed world he grew up in.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Skating rink hits and hustling haircuts at the barbershop
segments.summary: Hiding blues records from the preacher, big-band hits at the skating rink, and selling his place in the barbershop line with his cousins.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Extended family and church life
segments.summary: Baker describes his large close-knit extended family on both sides and a childhood of all-day Baptist church services and storefront churches.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Elementary school, school music and May Day
segments.summary: He attended Francis Parker (P.S. 56), sang in school choirs, and remembers May Day programs, vaccinations and lifelong friends from first grade.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Indianapolis
segments.title: Crispus Attucks High School and the feeder schools
segments.summary: The school was founded in 1927 under the Klan-era segregation pushed by D. C. Stephenson, with all black students from the east side and elsewhere funneled through feeder schools.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Early music at home: piano rolls, his sister's lessons, singing
segments.summary: His stepmother thought piano wrong for a boy, so he listened to his sister's lessons, pumped piano rolls and picked out boogie-woogie.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: First instruments: trombone, E-flat tuba and the cigar-box fingering
segments.summary: In seventh grade he was handed a tuba instead of a trombone, lugged it home on the streetcar, and later got a sousaphone from Mr. Brown at Attucks.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Cousin Walt's barbershop, bebop, Lester Young records and Dizzy Gillespie solos
segments.summary: He heard bebop all day at his cousin's barbershop, cousin Manson gave him Lester Young records, and his band mates learned Dizzy Gillespie heads.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Crispus Attucks teachers, black history and the school basketball dynasty
segments.summary: Attucks had unusually well-educated teachers, including Dr. Morton-Finney, taught black history, and later became a basketball power under Ray Crowe and Oscar Robertson.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Mr. Brown, Mr. Merrifield and the Rhythm Rockets
segments.summary: The Attucks music faculty, stock arrangements, the Rhythm Rockets, and Mr. Brown scolding him over the Pavanne bass line.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Playing the junior prom and learning swing riffs
segments.summary: The Rhythm Rockets' disastrous junior prom, and learning simple riffs like Intermission Riff to start jamming.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Sitting in at Indiana Avenue clubs as teenagers
segments.summary: Baker, Slide Hampton and other beginners sat in at jam sessions along Indiana Avenue alongside pros like Pookie Johnson, Jimmy Coe and the Montgomerys.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Practicing at the Hampton family house
segments.summary: The Hampton family band of Slide and his siblings let local youngsters rehearse at their house, where trombone parts were written as slide positions.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Getting lost on stage, bass trombone, getting into clubs, and Lockefield Gardens
segments.summary: He was abandoned on the stand while playing Zing Went the Strings of My Heart, switched to bass trombone, disguised himself to enter clubs, and describes Lockefield Gardens and the New Deal.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Sunset Terrace, Cotton Club and the Sky Club
segments.summary: Hearing Coltrane, Charlie Parker and J. J. Johnson with Illinois Jacquet at the Sunset Terrace and Cotton Club, and the after-hours Sky Club on Indiana Avenue.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: The years of Indiana Avenue's heyday
segments.summary: Baker dates the avenue's golden era to roughly 1946-1953 and notes its history as a black district.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: The older Indianapolis musicians, Eldridge Morrison's band and transcribing Atomic Basie
segments.summary: Older players such as Roger Jones and Jimmy Coe; his first work was with Eldridge Morrison's band, for whom he transcribed Atomic Basie for $15 a chart.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Monk Montgomery, the Fender bass and the Lionel Hampton harbor story
segments.summary: Monk Montgomery's role in the invention of the Fender bass and the story of jumping into the harbor for $10 while with Lionel Hampton.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Strengths and gaps in his school music training
segments.summary: The school gave good theory and ensemble training but lacked strings, bassoons and up-to-date equipment.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: The YMCA band and the standards teachers set
segments.summary: Playing in the YMCA band on parts that bore the names of J. J. Johnson and Jimmy Coe, and the high expectations placed on Attucks students.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Extended family and the community's watch over children
segments.summary: Everyone in the neighborhood acted as family, which Baker links to the sense of responsibility among musicians.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Learning from older musicians by imitation
segments.summary: Older players taught by imitation; Wes Montgomery told him he would hear it, and Slide Hampton wrote out positions.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Teaching Freddie Hubbard and the Indianapolis players who left
segments.summary: He taught Freddie Hubbard to read, the pair learned Donna Lee in secret, and he recalls Hubbard's first album and Leroy Vinnegar's success in Los Angeles.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Deciding to play jazz
segments.summary: Baker knew from high school he would play jazz, and describes how realistic that career then seemed.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Playing professionally with Eldridge Morrison at the Indiana Roof
segments.summary: His first professional work with Eldridge Morrison in high school, including a laughing fit with Slide Hampton at the Indiana Roof.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Working nights as a busboy while in high school
segments.summary: He bused tables at LaRue's, the Plantation and other clubs, then sat in until 3 a.m., and fell asleep in Mr. Morton-Finney's French class.

segments.chapter: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
segments.title: Playing at LaRue's, a flying mallet at the Plantation and getting fired over Muzak
segments.summary: Baker was allowed to play with Denny Dutton's band in his busboy jacket, saw Buddy Montgomery knock out a drunk, and was fired for requesting Muzak tunes.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: A year at Arthur Jordan Conservatory and being sent away from Butler
segments.summary: After high school he spent a year at Butler's Arthur Jordan Conservatory, was expelled for dancing with a white girl, and Dr. Roscoe Polin helped him enter Indiana University.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Busboy earnings and a bad tour with Mr. Hibbert
segments.summary: LaRue's tips made him well off, but a tour with Slide Hampton and Mr. Hibbert paid $20 and ended with a stolen wallet.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Arthur Jordan Conservatory: baritone horn and work at LaRue's
segments.summary: At Arthur Jordan he played baritone horn in the concert band as its only black member while continuing to work next door at LaRue's.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Arthur Jordan jazz band, the short Kenton stint and the move to Indiana University
segments.summary: Don Kelly recommended Baker to finish a Stan Kenton tour, where he met Curtis Counce, Mel Lewis and Pepper Adams, before he entered Indiana University full-time in 1950.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Jazz at Indiana University in the early 1950s
segments.summary: IU in 1951-53 had a hotbed of jam sessions with Jerry Coker and Al Kiger, visits from Cannonball Adderley, and Fred Dale's band that entered the first collegiate Metronome contest.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: The Fred Dale band's recording and summer at Lake Hamilton
segments.summary: Baker wrote the Mean to Me arrangement for the Metronome contest record, then played a six-week resort engagement at Lake Hamilton with weekend trips to Detroit.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Classical training at IU and the Indianapolis Symphony audition
segments.summary: Baker earned degrees at IU and played bass trombone in the orchestra, but Fabien Sevitzky's praise at his audition made clear no board would hire a black player.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Segregation in Bloomington and President Herman B. Wells
segments.summary: Black students could not live in dorms, eat in town restaurants or get haircuts, though Herman B. Wells began dismantling segregation.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: The orchestra's Carnegie Hall trip, living with athletes and mixed bands
segments.summary: A restaurant refusal on the orchestra trip, Ernst Hoffman's response, roommate Milt Campbell and the racially mixed fraternity jobs and jam sessions.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Jazz as an extracurricular activity and Ernst Hoffman's Till Eulenspiegel remark
segments.summary: Jazz was not part of the School of Music curriculum, and Baker recalls Hoffman correcting his Straight No Chaser practice with the Till Eulenspiegel melody.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Traverse City summer job, Indianapolis gigs and the move to Los Angeles
segments.summary: After a six-week job at Traverse City, Baker played with Wes Montgomery and led a Modern Jazz Septet before heading to Los Angeles with little money.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Hungry in Los Angeles and the telegram from Lincoln University
segments.summary: Nearly starving, he fainted at a pancake house, then received a telegram offering him a one-year job at Lincoln University.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Arriving at Lincoln University in a flowered shirt
segments.summary: He arrived in a snowstorm in pink pants, was teased by students including Julius Hemphill, and was told jazz was not allowed in the building.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Teaching at Lincoln: Leroy Ingram and Smokey Smith and his Harlem Aces
segments.summary: As a hard first-year teacher he assigned too much to Leroy Ingram's class, and led a rhythm-and-blues group on Sundays in Columbia, Missouri.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Lincoln campus life: overheard remarks, a jazz concert and dating rules
segments.summary: He overheard teachers mocking him in the cafeteria line, staged a jazz concert, and learned the school's sundown rules for dating.

segments.chapter: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
segments.title: Lincoln students, marrying Jeannie across the state line and weeks with Lionel Hampton
segments.summary: He sent Felicia Weathers to IU, married Jeannie in Chicago because of Missouri miscegenation laws, and returned to IU in 1957 after short stints with Lionel Hampton.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: Back at Indiana University, first jazz students and paying his way
segments.summary: At IU in 1957 his first jazz students included Freddie Hubbard and Charles Tyler, and gigs paying $13 covered his room and board.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: Jeannie joins him, birth of April, and forming a big band and septet
segments.summary: Jeannie moved to Bloomington, daughter April was born in August 1958, and Baker formed a big band and small group while finishing his degree.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: Families' reactions to the marriage and the big band's 1959 rise
segments.summary: His family was relaxed, Jeannie's parents disowned her until April's birth, and his big band won the Notre Dame Jazz Festival in 1959.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: Gunther Schuller's 'Indiana Renaissance' article, Wes Montgomery and the Lenox invitation
segments.summary: Schuller heard Baker's big band and Wes Montgomery at the Missile Room and wrote the article, leading to Lenox scholarships; Baker also describes Roland Kirk sitting in.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: Arriving at the Lenox School of Jazz and the Ornette Coleman dispute
segments.summary: Baker and his friends arrived late to Lenox, found Ornette Coleman had already unsettled the school, and argued daily with George Russell about playing without changes.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: Jazz in the Space Age and George Russell forming a sextet
segments.summary: Baker played bass trombone on Russell's Jazz in the Space Age, then Russell came to Indianapolis to teach the quartet his music.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: The Russell sextet takes shape and opens at the Five Spot
segments.summary: After the Notre Dame festival win, the group became the George Russell Sextet and played New York's Five Spot where Miles, Coltrane and Rollins came to listen.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: Mingus at the Lenox Inn, the School of Jazz and the Russell albums
segments.summary: A late-night jam session where Mingus criticized Baker's playing, Baker's description of the School of Jazz, and the sextet's recordings for Riverside and Decca.

segments.chapter: Return to IU, Lenox and the George Russell Sextet
segments.title: Lenox 1960 and hearing Kind of Blue for the first time
segments.summary: Back at Lenox with the sextet, Baker studied with J. J. Johnson and heard Kind of Blue first, mistaking Wynton Kelly for Bill Evans.

segments.chapter: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
segments.title: The 1953 car accident and the dislocated jaw that ended his trombone playing
segments.summary: Thrown through a windshield returning from Lake Hamilton, Baker spent a week in a coma, then years later discovered he had played on a dislocated jaw and had to quit trombone around 1960-61.

segments.chapter: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
segments.title: Hospital stays, the psychiatric ward anecdote, then piano, bass and cello
segments.summary: He tried to play long tones in a hospital ward, then practiced piano and bass and was given a pawn-shop cello by Mr. Brown.

segments.chapter: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
segments.title: When Baker began writing and the pieces for the Russell sextet
segments.summary: He wrote for the big band in 1959 but only took writing seriously after leaving the horn, contributing Kentucky Oysters, Lunacy and other pieces to George Russell's sextet.

segments.chapter: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
segments.title: Thelonious Monk at the Five Spot and the Cincinnati ballpark
segments.summary: Monk said Baker looked like him in 1962 and, two years later in Cincinnati, that Baker was uglier; Baker also begins describing his early cello struggles.

segments.chapter: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
segments.title: Learning cello in Indianapolis and the old gang's jam sessions
segments.summary: Starting cello was hard, but sessions with Elvin Jones and the old Russell players helped; he also recalls playing piano for Slide Hampton and Freddie Hubbard.

segments.chapter: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
segments.title: Ted Dunbar, Wes Montgomery and a night at the 19th Hole
segments.summary: Guitarist Ted Dunbar came to Indianapolis in 1959, became Baker's friend and student, and tried to challenge Wes Montgomery in a story Baker tells.

segments.chapter: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
segments.title: Cello versus trombone and the teachers Teraspulsky and Winold
segments.summary: Cello did not draw on his trombone hearing, and only strict lessons from Leopold Teraspulsky and Helga Winold fixed his fundamentals.

segments.chapter: Composing and the Black Music Center
segments.title: Early compositions he regrets and the piano sonata
segments.summary: Baker wishes he could retract his first twenty years of compositions and discusses the piano sonata that became the subject of two dissertations.

segments.chapter: Composing and the Black Music Center
segments.title: George Russell's Lydian concept as a compositional influence
segments.summary: Baker explains how Russell mentored the sextet and why the Lydian concept is a theory that leads practice.

segments.chapter: Composing and the Black Music Center
segments.title: The German radio question and the 22nd Psalm cantata
segments.summary: A Stuttgart interviewer asked him about the Lydian concept in German, and after his father's death in 1964 he wrote his first serious work, a cantata on the 22nd Psalm.

segments.chapter: Composing and the Black Music Center
segments.title: Liturgical works, the first violin concerto and Dr. King's assassination
segments.summary: He wrote masses and a violin-and-jazz-band concerto for Josef Gingold, and after King's death learned there was no black chamber music at IU, leading to the Black Music Center.

segments.chapter: Composing and the Black Music Center
segments.title: Black music seminars and the Black Composer Series
segments.summary: Interviews, seminars and the Columbia Black Composer Series grew out of the Black Music Center, along with black studies programs around the country.

segments.chapter: Composing and the Black Music Center
segments.title: The abandoned Malcolm X opera, many concertos and third stream
segments.summary: Baker dropped an opera with Mari Evans on advice of Juan Orrego-Salas, wrote concertos for many soloists, and discusses third stream and twelve-tone influences.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Hired in 1966 to build the IU jazz program
segments.summary: Baker was hired after Bill Russo declined, started with a handful of courses, got jazz band accepted as a major ensemble and taught huge civil-rights-era courses.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Hiring faculty, writing for the bands and the Down Beat 'Neglected Stepchild' article
segments.summary: He hired George Ross and Dominic Spera, wrote much of the bands' music, and withdrew from contests after his 1964 article on unqualified jazz teachers.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Non-competitive festivals, summer camps and a mission of service
segments.summary: Baker favors non-competitive festivals and camps, recalls Quincy Jones and Cannonball at a mentoring festival, and lists his notable students.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Early NEA panels and lobbying for jazz funding
segments.summary: From 1968 Baker served on NEA panels and argued that Basie and Woody Herman bands deserved subsidy like symphony orchestras, with Cannonball Adderley backing him.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Cannonball's exit, Kennedy Center, the National Council and the IU alliance
segments.summary: He chaired the Kennedy Center jazz advisory committee, was appointed to the National Council on the Arts, helped found the National Jazz Service Organization, and tied jazz to the music school.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Inherited students, school rankings and recommending other programs
segments.summary: Students Jerry Coker sent to Baker's Sunday lessons were the program's first recruits, and he advised applicants to ask students and consider other schools.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Jazz education pioneers and the first improvisation books
segments.summary: Baker with Jerry Coker, Dan Haerle and others wrote the first jazz method books on a blank field and were later often plagiarized.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Jamey Aebersold's play-alongs and the unsung high-school teachers
segments.summary: Aebersold personalized Music Minus One for jazz, and Baker credits unsung teachers at schools such as Cass Tech and Crispus Attucks.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Imitation, assimilation, innovation and caring for older musicians
segments.summary: Baker defends jazz education against the robot charge, says players pass through imitation to their own voice, and worries about aged musicians without pensions.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: The American Jazz Masters award and its $20,000 stipend
segments.summary: Baker recalls how the NEA Jazz Masters award began, how Antoinette Handy tied it to the jazz educators' convention, and why the unchanged $20,000 value is naive.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Missed Medal of Arts honorees and the value of the oral history project
segments.summary: The National Council missed Miles Davis and Sarah Vaughan for the Medal of Arts; Baker praises the Smithsonian oral history project, citing J. J. Johnson, and the importance of the Jazz Masters.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Little recognition or funding for jazz compared with other arts
segments.summary: Jazz gets scant recognition on the Grammys and from BET and foundations, though the North Sea festival and Denmark's Jazzpar Prize do better.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Day two opens; why Europe embraced jazz and why musicians became expatriates
segments.summary: On June 20 Lida asks about support for jazz abroad; Baker explains European scholarship, the exotic appeal that drew expatriates, and why novelty fades into nationalism.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Jazz education creates a consumer market; government support abroad
segments.summary: America leads in jazz education and audiences while lagging in public support compared with Canada, Australia and Europe's radio orchestras.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: American prudishness about the NEA and overseas jobs disappearing
segments.summary: The NEA retreated after the Maplethorpe and Serrano controversies, and European radio jobs for Americans like Jiggs Whigham are vanishing as nationalism grows.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: Race, exoticism and tolerance toward Black musicians in Europe
segments.summary: Europeans accepted jazz musicians as exotics, like Josephine Baker and Bricktop, but once they became locals the welcome cooled.

segments.chapter: Building the IU jazz program, jazz education and abroad
segments.title: The NEA backlash and public arts funding abroad
segments.summary: After the Serrano controversy the NEA cut individual grants, and other countries such as Japan and Italy spend far more per capita.

segments.chapter: The Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra
segments.title: Origins of the Smithsonian orchestra from the Jazz Masterworks Editions project
segments.summary: Fred Starr's idea of urtext Ellington and Henderson editions led through Roger Kennedy, Gunther Schuller and John Hasse to an orchestra in residence.

segments.chapter: The Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra
segments.title: Forming the orchestra in 1991 and the move to concept concerts
segments.summary: The orchestra started with hodgepodge concerts under John Hasse and Dottie Green, then did concept programs, and Baker and Schuller differed about treating the music as museum pieces.

segments.chapter: The Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra
segments.title: First-year concerts at Carmichael Hall and playing for Congress
segments.summary: The orchestra gave about eleven concerts its first year at Carmichael Hall, and played on Capitol Hill during the Clarence Thomas hearings.

segments.chapter: The Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra
segments.title: Other repertory orchestras and the Smithsonian's government backing
segments.summary: Columbus's Jazz Arts Group and Jim Ketch's orchestra also played repertory, but the Smithsonian alone had government support and played the White House.

segments.chapter: The Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra
segments.title: Rethinking repertory: what 'masterworks' means
segments.summary: With James Zimmerman and Ken Kimery the orchestra reexamined its premise, since fans can buy originals, and widened its scope after Andy Jacobs's remark about a curving road.

segments.chapter: The Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra
segments.title: Inclusiveness and Gunther Schuller's departure
segments.summary: Baker explains the orchestra now mixes pristine repertory with contemporary work, and that Schuller left voluntarily over differences in direction.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Other jazz service: the National Jazz Service Organization
segments.summary: Baker describes the National Jazz Service Organization, the book New Perspectives in Jazz and saying yes to every promotion effort.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Why Lenox cannot be replicated: comparing Monaco and Steans Institute
segments.summary: Baker explains Lenox's unique all-star faculty and complete curriculum, unlike the performance-focused programs at Monaco and Ravinia's Steans Institute.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: The Ravinia Steans Institute jazz week
segments.summary: Baker describes choosing advanced young players, using original music suggested by Nathan Davis, and calls the week his most rewarding educational experience.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: The Thelonious Monk Institute's rotating faculty
segments.summary: The Monk Institute hosts small classes at an existing school with a different star teacher each week, unlike Tanglewood's daily contact.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Can young players still find mentors? Democratization of jazz knowledge
segments.summary: Baker says students can find help in New York, colleges and camps, and compares jazz books and records to the printing press ending an aristocracy of knowledge.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: People who influenced him
segments.summary: Baker names his parents, Russell Brown, LaVerne Newsome, J. J. Johnson, Slide Hampton, George Russell and his own students as influences.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: White House invitations and the Lionel Hampton party
segments.summary: From Carter to Reagan Baker attended White House events, including a cheaply done, politically motivated tent party for Lionel Hampton.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Jazz as a metaphor for democracy at the White House
segments.summary: Baker helped plan a White House program and explains how a jazz band balances leader and collective, with a nod to integrated bands like Artie Shaw's.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Tipper Gore, the 'national treasure' statement and keeping jazz visible
segments.summary: Baker praises Tipper Gore's sincerity, says the National Jazz Service Organization drafted the congressional statement making jazz a national treasure, and urges staying visible to presidents.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: A short stint with Lionel Hampton
segments.summary: Baker played only two weeks and part of a tour with Hampton in the mid-1950s because the pay was bad and the personnel constantly changed.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: A tour with Maynard Ferguson
segments.summary: Slide Hampton got Baker onto Ferguson's band for the rest of a tour, where he met Lanny Morgan, Willie Maiden and Bobby Timmons and became lifelong friends with Maynard.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Joining Quincy Jones's European band tour
segments.summary: On George Russell's recommendation Baker joined Quincy Jones's band after two rehearsals in a section with Melba Liston and Curtis Fuller, and was listed on a bootleg as 'plus one other trombone'.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: First trip abroad and sitting in at European clubs
segments.summary: The Quincy Jones tour was Baker's first time out of the U.S.; he sat in at clubs and met Bud Powell and others.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Russell sextet personnel, Don Ellis and the Kansas City trip
segments.summary: Don Ellis replaced Al Kiger, and the sextet toured, recorded in Kansas City, played Birdland and the Museum of Modern Art, and won Baker the Down Beat New Star Award.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Eric Dolphy, Steve Swallow and the album Ezz-thetic
segments.summary: Steve Swallow and Eric Dolphy joined the band, which rehearsed daily and recorded all night; Baker was replaced by Brian Trentham when his jaw failed.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: George Russell's importance and learning tunes quickly with Wes
segments.summary: Baker calls the Russell band the biggest event in his career and says playing with Wes Montgomery meant learning five tunes before a gig.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Two years without an instrument and the wired jaw
segments.summary: Without a playable instrument he played gigs on piano under heavy medication, had his jaw wired for six weeks, and began cello with Mr. Brown's encouragement.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Playing trombone again in 1971 and recording Living Time
segments.summary: His trombone returned for a time and he recorded Gettin' It Together and Living Time, where George Russell credited Baker's Schizophrenic for the idea of Events.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Bill Evans: Living Time and later years
segments.summary: Baker describes the all-star Living Time date, his talks with Bill Evans about William Blake, and Evans's decline and death.

segments.chapter: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
segments.title: Giving up the trombone for good
segments.summary: Baker returned to cello, and the doctors' warning about losing his facial muscles and barbecue persuaded him to stop playing trombone.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Resuming; his own working groups after coming to IU in 1966
segments.summary: After the break Baker explains he kept playing with Indianapolis musicians for a year or two after moving to Bloomington, then formed bass and cello groups and a string quartet.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: The 21st Century Bebop Band and Laurel Records
segments.summary: From the mid-1970s the 21st Century Bebop Band with Harvey Phillips and Jim Beard made records for Hershel Gilbert's Laurel label, which also issued his classical works.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Later versions of the Bebop Band and its personnel
segments.summary: Baker names the successive lineups, including Bob Hurst, Shawn Pelton, Ralph Bowen, Jack Wilkins and a later group with Lida Baker, Tom Gullion and Luke Gillespie.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Steppin' Out, opening for Dizzy Gillespie and his cello career
segments.summary: He records Steppin' Out for Liscio, opened for Dizzy Gillespie and Maynard Ferguson at Bloomington, and keeps performing as a cellist at Bear's Place and camps.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: The concerti: saxophone, bass, tuba, cello and others
segments.summary: Baker lists his 14 or 15 commissioned concertos, written for soloists such as Dominic Spera, Gary Karr, Harvey Phillips, Janos Starker and Lee Konitz.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Recordings of his chamber works and Roots II
segments.summary: Starker and Anne Akiko Meyers recorded his sonatas, and the piano trio Roots II for the Beaux Arts Trio is his best-known work.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Orchestral, chamber and choral works and their recordings
segments.summary: Baker lists recordings of Le Chat qui Peche, his sonatas, Kosbro ('keep on steppin', brothers'), Life Cycles and Alabama Landscape, totaling 60 to 70 albums.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Jazz recordings, Black America and Ellingtones for Dexter Gordon
segments.summary: He cites albums by his groups, Charles Tyler and Russell, plus Black America written after King's death and Ellingtones, the last work Dexter Gordon recorded.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: About 2,000 compositions, publishers and companion pieces
segments.summary: Baker has close to 2,000 compositions, 200 published, including companion pieces such as Homage a l'Histoire and Life Cycles for existing odd-instrumentation works.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Known only as a classical composer; the ballet Masque of the Red Death
segments.summary: A listener at SMU did not know he wrote jazz; Baker also mentions a new ballet, percussion piece and Top Brass commission up to June 2000.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Writing on commission and choosing texts: the Bible, Mari Evans and Dunbar
segments.summary: Baker prefers commissions with set parameters and chooses texts mainly from the Bible, Mari Evans and Paul Laurence Dunbar, including works for the Fisk Jubilee Singers.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Film and television scoring and Quincy Jones's pitch to move to Hollywood
segments.summary: He scored The Black Frontier and The Trial of Captain Henry Flipper, and Quincy Jones urged him to go to Hollywood to study with Earle Hagen.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Influences as a composer: Bartok, Ellington and finding ethnic sources
segments.summary: Baker names Bartok on the classical side and Ellington, Russell, J. J. and Gil Evans on the jazz side, and describes his breakthrough from twelve-tone writing to using blues and spirituals.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Always listening: the Smithsonian orchestra as preservation and nurturing
segments.summary: Baker listens to music daily and says conducting the Smithsonian orchestra balances preserving the best of jazz with his teaching work.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Desert island recordings and books
segments.summary: Baker would take Nat King Cole, Massey Hall, Bartok's Concerto for Orchestra, Ellington's Far East Suite and a J. J. Johnson big band record, plus the Bible, Poe and Lerone Bennett.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: What he would do with unlimited resources
segments.summary: With unlimited money Baker would record everything he writes with the best orchestras, since recordings are one's legacy.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie as mentor
segments.summary: Dizzy gave Baker the Lenox scholarship, wrote him letters and a recommendation, and always asked Baker's band to open for him.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Ted Dunbar as his closest friend
segments.summary: Baker calls Ted Dunbar his brother and says no one outside his family was closer, from about 1959 until Dunbar's death.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Short tributes: Wes Montgomery, Slide Hampton and Eric Dolphy
segments.summary: Baker calls Wes the greatest jazz guitarist, Slide his alter ego and best trombonist in the business, and Dolphy an unrealized talent who died at 34.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: J. J. Johnson as idol and friend
segments.summary: Baker describes J. J. Johnson as his idol on trombone, a close friend and one of the last surviving bebop pioneers.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: James Moody's phone call
segments.summary: Moody phoned Baker's office in the early 1970s asking how to use his books, and the two became close friends.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Charles Suber of Down Beat
segments.summary: Suber judged Baker at Notre Dame, taught him to say thank you, and published his first book and many Down Beat pieces.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
