segments.title: Charles Colin's help after the move to New York
segments.summary: When Baker moved to New York in 1977-78, Charles Colin paid him to write books, gave him studio space and took him under his wing.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Dan Morgenstern and honest jazz writing
segments.summary: Baker respects Morgenstern and Don DeMicheal as honest critics, and recalls Morgenstern supplying music for a Roy Eldridge commission overnight.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Janos Starker
segments.summary: Baker calls Starker the greatest cellist, whose 1949 Kodaly recording set the standard, and says political disagreements do not affect their friendship.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Day three begins; Harvey Phillips and The Golden Striker
segments.summary: On June 21 Lida resumes the list of friends; Baker met tubist Harvey Phillips on the all-brass Golden Striker album and later wrote him a tuba and string quartet piece.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Harvey Phillips as a model of efficiency and teaching
segments.summary: Baker admires Phillips for never procrastinating, his teaching philosophy, his role in the 21st Century Bebop Band, and a pun-filled tuba concerto written for him.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Meeting Gunther Schuller at Tanglewood and at Indiana University
segments.summary: Baker met Schuller through the Met Opera tour at IU and then Lenox, and took him to hear Wes Montgomery before the 'Indiana Renaissance' article.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Gunther Schuller's friendship and the offer to head New England Conservatory jazz
segments.summary: Schuller and Baker stayed close friends, Schuller tried to hire him for NEC in the late 1960s, and he joined the Smithsonian orchestra.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Dominic Spera, friend and colleague at Indiana University
segments.summary: Spera came back as Baker's teaching assistant, taught at Eau Claire, and joined IU in 1977 to run the jazz program with Baker for twenty years.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Larry Ridley, from IU violinist to New York bassist
segments.summary: Baker recruited Larry Ridley to IU, where he switched from violin to bass, played in the 1958-59 big band, then played with Sonny Rollins and Monk and led the Rutgers program.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Jerry Coker and parallel careers in jazz education
segments.summary: Baker has known Coker since 1950; the two wrote overlapping books, Coker recommended him for the IU job, and they differed in blues versus Ellington tastes and output.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Jerry Coker's later career, Tanglewood and Harry Kraut's Monaco school
segments.summary: Coker toured with Aebersold camps, and Harry Kraut, Bernstein's manager, brought the 1992 Monaco festival to IU because of Baker, who hired an all-star faculty.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Jamey Aebersold: student, play-alongs and summer camps
segments.summary: Aebersold studied with Baker in New Albany days, launched the play-along records, took over the national stage band camps, and together with Baker and Coker formed 'the ABCs of jazz'.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Nathan Davis and the Pittsburgh jazz program
segments.summary: A letter from Nathan Davis arrived just after Pittsburgh asked Baker for a jazz program head, and the two stayed close, working together at Ravinia and Monaco.

segments.chapter: His own groups, compositions and friends
segments.title: Charles Tyler: avant-garde student and friend
segments.summary: Tyler studied with Baker, recorded Eastern Man Alone, taught him to avoid practicing tunes, and housed him in Brooklyn in 1978.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Baker's affinity with the avant garde, Stanley Crouch and the AACM
segments.summary: Besides the Russell group, Baker played with loft-scene avant-gardists, interviewed AACM members, and recalls Russell's 'last refuge of the untalented' remark and the Art Ensemble in Stockholm.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Muhal Richard Abrams and Lester Bowie
segments.summary: Baker followed the Art Ensemble of Chicago in Australia and calls Muhal Richard Abrams a close friend and genius.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Dating his avant-garde period and a free-form first years at IU
segments.summary: The avant-garde work ran through the Russell years, free playing in Indianapolis with Elvin Jones and spatial pieces in his first IU years, though he grew more conservative with age.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: The circle of Black classical composers: Hale Smith, T. J. Anderson and Olly Wilson
segments.summary: Baker names William Grant Still, Ulysses Kay and Coleridge-Taylor Perkinson among the black composers he met and interviewed through the Black Music Center and the Columbia series.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: The Black Composers series and performances by major orchestras
segments.summary: The Columbia series had few residual effects, though Baker's works were played by the New York Philharmonic and others, and he helps younger composers; George Walker won the Pulitzer.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Few opportunities for Black composers and orchestral players
segments.summary: Baker says little has changed: black composers get programmed in February, few Black players are in major orchestras, and top conductors seldom perform his works.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: The Black Music Center at IU: collections and conferences
segments.summary: Dean Wilfred Bain backed the center founded after King's death, which collected scores by black composers and ran conferences that produced books and performances of Black America.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Other schools' programs, the 'special' stigma and a second renaissance
segments.summary: Baker describes the wave of black music programs nationwide, their dependence on grants, Cecil Taylor's failing grades at Wisconsin, and wanting to be in subscription series, not special events.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Confrontation versus conciliation as strategy
segments.summary: Baker argues progress on race has come under pressure, that strategies must fit the time, and that gender equality follows the same pattern.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Witnessing a lynching and why performers wore a mask
segments.summary: Baker saw a lynching as a child, defends Stepin Fetchit and Billie Holiday for accommodating, and describes the 'Money, Missionary, Marines' theme in Black America.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Artists as the conscience of the nation: Dr. King, Through This Vale of Tears and Dunbar
segments.summary: Baker explains how composers respond to events like the King assassination, citing Through This Vale of Tears, the poem Now That He Is Safely Dead, and Paul Robeson and Dunbar.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: 1960s sit-ins at Indiana University
segments.summary: He recalls campus sit-ins, occupying the Little 500 track and the price speakers like Orlando Taylor paid for protest.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: The Malcolm X opera and The Meeting
segments.summary: Baker passed on a Malcolm X opera for time reasons but found the two-man play The Meeting between Malcolm and King attractive.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Dr. King, the Holocaust and the Middle Passage
segments.summary: Baker recalls hearing King the night before his death and says slavery's middle passages deserve an opera as much as the Holocaust.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Hearing Malcolm X speak and the poem Alabama Landscape
segments.summary: Baker heard Malcolm on Harlem street corners, and explains Alabama Landscape, Mari Evans's poem about Michael Taylor's death in a police car in Indianapolis.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Calling the muse: advice from teachers
segments.summary: Baker recommends Koestler and Nachmanovitch, recounts writing Kosbro in an auditorium, Donald Erb's daily writing hours, and the difference between a song and a theme.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Testing a theme and word play
segments.summary: He turns a theme upside down and sideways to test whether it can bear fruit, and uses puns and word play as exercises in changing context.

segments.chapter: The avant garde, race and the artist's voice
segments.title: Changing context in improvising: quotes and reusing material
segments.summary: In his own playing he combines tunes and quotes, forces himself out of comfort, and says a theme changes meaning with context like hair in butter.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Living in Los Angeles and in Harlem with Slide Hampton
segments.summary: Baker briefly lived in Los Angeles, then in Harlem behind the Apollo with Slide Hampton, going to jam sessions nightly.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Second New York stay with the Russell band
segments.summary: Back in New York with George Russell, Baker lived with Chuck Israels and at the 34th Street YMCA while playing clubs.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Third New York stay: Brooklyn, Rutgers and remarriage
segments.summary: On sabbatical in 1977-78 Baker lived at 190 Carlton Avenue with Charles Tyler, taught at Charles Colin Studios and Rutgers, and married Lida.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Why he started writing books
segments.summary: Baker began writing books because he needed information to play and teach, starting with the improvisation and arranging books.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Philosophical essays, lectures and books still in his head
segments.summary: He wrote essays like 'Jazz: the Academy's Neglected Stepchild', lectured widely, and has several unwritten books on teaching and Third Stream writing.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Attribution, plagiarism and the importance of an index
segments.summary: Baker checks books for his name in the index, recalls Ted Dunbar scolding a student for borrowing, and values a teacher's recall.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Challenging students and practicing in odd keys
segments.summary: Students such as Ralph Bowen and Delfayo Marsalis forced him to invent exercises, and he describes practicing every tune in one key and the 34 bebop tunes.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Building vocabulary cumulatively and the tune-phrase games
segments.summary: Baker explains why vocabulary should be reusable, as with tunes sharing Take the A Train changes, and plays singing games like Joy Spring with the Cokers.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Challenging books and the Techniques of Improvisation series
segments.summary: He writes only challenging books, and Moody and Nathan Davis say they live in his Cycles volume.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: The growth of the jazz educators' association from NAJE to IAJE
segments.summary: Baker traces the organization from a mom-and-pop NAJE under MENC to IAJE with executive director Bill McFarlin and thousands of members, and his early alienation from it.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Becoming IAJE president-elect
segments.summary: Baker served as vice president, declined a presidency during earlier turmoil, and accepts the presidency-elect role at age 68.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: April's path from J. C. Penney buyer to music teacher
segments.summary: His daughter April graduated from IU's jazz program, worked as a J. C. Penney buyer, then returned to Bloomington to teach voice and violin; Baker also wrote a bicentennial piece for Penney.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: April's teaching method and granddaughter Kirsten's violin
segments.summary: April teaches singers step by step and imitation, and Baker bribes his granddaughter Kirsten to stay with violin.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Contributions and hopes for his legacy
segments.summary: Baker names education and classical music by Black composers as contributions, and wants to be remembered as someone easy to get along with.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Rather be remembered as a nice human being; Larry Bird and sportsmanship
segments.summary: Baker jokes about his early-morning practicing, says he wants to be remembered as a person who liked people, and objects to Larry Bird on hating opponents.

segments.chapter: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy
segments.title: Closing remarks and transcription notes
segments.summary: Baker jokes about the Lakers and thanks the interviewers; the transcript credits Barry Kernfeld and Lida Baker's 2007 editing.
